articles.title: When is Vertebral Body Tethering in a Patient With an Open Triradiate Cartilage a Good Idea?
articles.authors: Zale C, Boyce J, Oh T, Davuluri S, Nice E, Pahys JM, et al.
articles.population: Children and adolescents with early-onset scoliosis or adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with open triradiate cartilage undergoing vertebral body tethering
articles.sample_size: 115 patients (60 with early-onset scoliosis, 55 with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis)
articles.outcomes: Success rate (curves less than 35 degrees at follow-up), undercorrection rate, overcorrection rate, and reoperation rate
articles.take_home: Vertebral body tethering was successful in 56% of patients with open triradiate cartilage, with 29% experiencing undercorrection and 15% experiencing overcorrection. Larger initial spine curves and smaller correction amounts were associated with undercorrection, while smaller initial curves were associated with overcorrection.

articles.title: A Simplified Method for Talocalcaneal Coalition Excision.
articles.authors: Lam A, Hartman R, Coe KM, O'Sullivan M, Zide J, Riccio AI
articles.population: Children and adolescents undergoing talocalcaneal coalition excision
articles.sample_size: 48 patients (54 feet): 39 feet traditional technique, 15 feet simplified technique
articles.outcomes: Operative time, anaesthesia time, procedural cost, perioperative complications, and secondary procedures at mean 2.1 years follow-up
articles.take_home: A simplified technique using guide wires for talocalcaneal coalition removal reduced operating time by nearly half and cut costs by more than 50 percent, with no increase in complications or need for repeat surgery.

articles.title: Acute, chronic, and non-fracture-related compartment syndrome in children. A current concepts review.
articles.authors: Candusso F, De Salvo S, Cabrioli C, Bari LJ, Facchi R, Lanari E, et al.
articles.population: Children with acute, chronic, and non-fracture-related compartment syndrome
articles.outcomes: Diagnostic approaches, epidemiology, pathophysiology, prognosis, and treatment outcomes including fasciotomy and wound closure rates
articles.take_home: Early recognition of compartment syndrome in children should focus on behavioural signs such as anxiety, agitation, and increased pain rather than late-stage symptoms. Whilst children have good healing potential even after delayed surgery, prompt treatment is essential to prevent permanent disability and loss of limb function.

articles.title: Cell Saver Use is Not Associated With Increased Morbidity But Reflects Transfusion Burden in Pediatric Spinal Deformity Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.authors: Ortega DA, Levin-Carrion Y, Reyes JL, Geraghty E, Shi T, Peterson H, et al.
articles.population: Children undergoing spinal fusion surgery for spinal deformity
articles.outcomes: All-cause morbidity within 30 days, respiratory/renal/infectious complications, neurological complications, reoperation rates, discharge to home, and allogeneic transfusion rates
articles.take_home: Cell saver use during spinal fusion surgery in children did not increase overall complications or health problems. Patients who received more cell saver blood tended to have more complex surgery and higher transfusion needs, suggesting the cell saver reflected how much bleeding occurred rather than causing harm.

articles.title: Do Normal Early Ultrasound Findings Predict Normal Acetabular Development? A Study of Late-Presenting Dysplasia in Graf Type I Hips.
articles.authors: Shi J, Li Y, Fan C, Miao M, Zheng X, Wang Z
articles.population: Children with Graf type I hips on early ultrasound who had pelvic X-rays after 2 years of age
articles.outcomes: Acetabular dysplasia development by final radiographic follow-up (mean age 2.9 years); association between ultrasound features and dysplasia
articles.take_home: Some hips that look normal on early ultrasound, particularly those with a blunt bony rim edge, may still develop acetabular dysplasia as the child grows. Girls and hips with subtle ultrasound abnormalities may need closer monitoring to catch dysplasia early.

articles.title: Prevalence of Acetabular Dysplasia in Early Adolescents From the General Population: A Generation R Study.
articles.authors: de Vos-Jakobs S, Boel F, Chen D, van Haasteren JCM, Tolk JJ, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, et al.
articles.study_type: Cross-sectional prevalence study from a prospective population-based cohort
articles.population: Early adolescents from the general population in Rotterdam, Netherlands
articles.sample_size: 3896 participants with mean age 13.6 years (46.8% male)
articles.outcomes: Prevalence of acetabular dysplasia (defined as lateral centre-edge angle less than 20.0 degrees) and associations with sex, ethnicity and skeletal maturity
articles.take_home: About 6 in every 100 early adolescents have acetabular dysplasia, a hip socket shape that can lead to problems later. Children who are still growing have nearly three times higher rates than those whose bones are fully mature, suggesting this condition can develop during childhood growth rather than only being present from birth.

articles.title: Surface Topography and Machine Learning: Strides Towards Radiation-Free Scoliosis Assessment: A Systematic Review.
articles.authors: Brigato P, Palombi D, Reyes JL, De Salvatore S, Brigato L, Lombardi JM, et al.
articles.study_type: Systematic review of machine learning and surface topography studies
articles.sample_size: 5015 patients across 12 studies; more than 6000 trunk surface scans
articles.outcomes: Accuracy of machine learning models in estimating curve severity and predicting Cobb angle (coronal curve magnitude); mean absolute errors of approximately 3 to 6 degrees; sensitivities exceeding 0.9; curve-type classification performance; binary classification for screening
articles.take_home: Machine learning combined with surface topography (scanning the back without X-rays) can estimate scoliosis curve severity with reasonable accuracy, though it still needs larger studies before it can replace X-rays in routine clinical practice. Current evidence suggests this approach could be useful for screening and monitoring, but more research is needed to confirm its role in clinical care.

articles.title: Art and Pediatric Orthopaedics: The Silent Messenger: Visualizing Trust, Mobility, and Recovery in Pediatric Orthopaedic Care.
articles.authors: Brausch W, Belthur M, Belthur MV
articles.population: Not applicable - artwork analysis rather than patient study
articles.outcomes: Analysis of sculpture's themes including mobility, trust, vulnerability and recovery in paediatric orthopaedic care
articles.take_home: This study examines a famous sculpture called The Silent Messenger that represents paediatric orthopaedic care, exploring how it communicates messages of hope, support and healing to patients and families. The artwork symbolises the compassionate, collaborative approach central to helping children recover from orthopaedic conditions.

articles.title: Assessment of the plane of maximum curvature in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis using 3D ultrasound : an exploratory study.
articles.authors: Yang ZQ, Wu C, Zhou Y, Schlosser TPC, Gardner A, Castelein RM, et al.
articles.study_type: Exploratory study evaluating three ultrasound measurement methods
articles.population: Adolescents with right major thoracic idiopathic scoliosis, stratified by severity
articles.outcomes: Reliability and agreement of three methods for measuring the plane of maximum curvature using 3D ultrasound; ultrasound curve angles and plane orientation; correlations with coronal curvature and thoracic kyphosis
articles.take_home: 3D ultrasound can reliably measure scoliosis curvature without radiation, and the endplate-apex-endplate method is recommended for routine assessment in moderate and severe cases. The most accurate 3D ultrasound method showed strong agreement with another method and consistent results across different curve severities.

articles.title: Hip arthroplasty following proximal femoral tumour resection in children : the impact of age and articulation on implant survival and the outcomes following acetabular revision.
articles.authors: Baird CAE, Green N, Evans S, Kurisunkal V, Parry MC, Stevenson J
articles.population: Children aged 2 to 16 years who had hip replacement after surgical removal of a proximal femoral bone tumour
articles.outcomes: Implant survival rates, revision-free survival, modes of implant failure, outcomes after revision surgery
articles.take_home: Very young children (12 years and under) have a high risk of needing further surgery within the first 10 years after hip replacement, regardless of the type used. Older children (over 12 years) who receive a total hip replacement do better than those who receive a hemiarthroplasty, though total hip replacement carries a small risk of early dislocation.

articles.title: Does transposition osteotomy of the acetabulum alter the natural history of developmental dysplasia of the hip?
articles.authors: Tanaka S, Fujii M, Kawano S, Ueno M, Oba Y, Morimoto T
articles.population: Patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), borderline DDH (BDDH), or normal hips
articles.sample_size: 683 hips treated with transposition osteotomy of the acetabulum and 353 contralateral native hips
articles.outcomes: 20-year cumulative probability of failure (progression to Tonnis grade 3 or conversion to total hip arthroplasty) and progression of osteoarthritis
articles.take_home: For severe hip dysplasia, acetabular repositioning surgery improved long-term hip survival compared to no surgery, but for borderline dysplasia, surgery did not significantly reduce the risk of needing hip replacement, although it did slow osteoarthritis progression.

articles.title: Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgeon Use of Removable Splints for Common Pediatric Distal Radius and Fibula Fractures: A 10-year Update.
articles.authors: Rundell AN, Kazanjian AS, Samora EC, Floccari LV, Samora J
articles.population: Paediatric orthopaedic surgeons in North America
articles.outcomes: Use of removable splints, braces or boots versus casts for distal radius and fibula fractures; barriers to using removable devices
articles.take_home: Surgeons are now much more likely to use removable devices for stable distal radius buckle fractures in children compared to 10 years ago (88% versus 29%), but family preference and concerns about compliance remain the main barriers to wider adoption of this approach.

articles.title: Web Creep Reoperation Following Simple Syndactyly Release Using Full-Thickness Skin Grafts and Skin Graft-Sparing Local Flaps.
articles.authors: Brickman BJ, Burke C, Rivera-Ramirez C, White SM, O'Shaughnessy M, Kluemper C, et al.
articles.population: Children under 18 years with simple syndactyly (webbed fingers) who had surgery to separate the fingers
articles.sample_size: 42 patients with 66 webbed spaces (32 treated with local flaps, 34 with skin grafts)
articles.outcomes: Need for repeat surgery due to web creep (the web reforming after surgery)
articles.take_home: Both local flaps and skin grafts worked equally well for treating simple syndactyly, with similar rates of about 30-34% needing repeat surgery over an average of 7 years. This suggests surgeons do not need to use skin grafts if local flaps can be used, as both have comparable web creep rates.

articles.title: Clinical outcomes after surgical treatment of open thigh muscular tears in skeletally immature patients.
articles.authors: Turati M, Mosca A, Crippa M, Tercier S, Leone G, Nicolaou N, et al.
articles.population: Skeletally immature patients with open thigh muscular lacerations treated surgically
articles.outcomes: Wound contamination, muscle involvement, complications, quality of life scores (Euro Quality of Life 5-Dimension, Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee, Simple Knee Value, Tegner Activity score), return to sport, reinjury rates at minimum 1-year follow-up
articles.take_home: Open thigh muscle tears in young people, commonly from ski accidents, can be treated very successfully with prompt surgery and early rehabilitation. Patients achieved excellent function scores and returned to sport without further injury.

articles.title: Patients' choice of healthcare provider for primary hip and knee arthroplasty: a national register-based observational cohort study of 62,676 patients from Norway, 2014-2018.
articles.authors: Hauglann B, Kjaervik C, Stensland E, Tesfay Y, Fenstad AM, Furnes O, et al.
articles.population: Patients undergoing elective primary hip and knee arthroplasty in Norway
articles.outcomes: Patients' willingness to travel (in minutes) for arthroplasty based on provider attributes including dedicated elective units, regional health authority location, surgical volume, proximity of adult children, and waiting times. Associations between travel preferences and patient characteristics including age, comorbidity, education and income.
articles.take_home: Patients were willing to travel significantly longer for certain provider features, particularly for dedicated elective surgical units (average 2 hours 36 minutes extra travel). However, older patients, those with serious health conditions, and those with lower education or income were less willing to travel, suggesting that choice of hospital for joint replacement surgery is influenced by both healthcare system features and patient circumstances.
